    Diagram 3 of 7

    Time-aware validation

    A race is a time series, so every model trains on earlier laps and is judged on later ones.

    • A shuffled K-fold would train on lap 50 and validate on lap 10 — leaking the future.
    • Folds choose hyperparameters and thresholds; the test laps are used once, at the end.
    • Practicals 6, 7, 8 and the quantum models all use this same split.

    How the recommendation is decided

    The decision rule inside _combine_recommendation.

    Did a rule assert pit_decision?
    yes
    Use the rule's verdictconfidence: high
    no
    Are both ML and DL pit predictions available?
    yes
    Do they predict the same class?
    yes
    Use the shared classconfidence: high if both are ≥ 0.1 from their cut-off, else moderate
    no
    Use ML (tie-break), flag disagreementconfidence: low
    no
    Use whichever one existsconfidence: moderate · none if neither
    Is the verdict “pit”?
    yes
    PIT NOW — or PIT IN N LAPS, where N is the first PIT step of the A* planconfidence:
    no
    STAY OUTconfidence:
    • Rules win because they encode knowledge one dry race cannot teach a model (safety cars, weather).
    • Cut-offs differ: DL uses its tuned threshold; the live ML class comes from predict(), i.e. 0.5.

    Practical 1 of 10 · app/intelligence/knowledge_representation/

    Knowledge Representation

    An F1 ontology and knowledge graph built from one declarative schema.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplicationsKey points & viva

    What and why

    Practical 1 models the Formula 1 domain explicitly: 61 entities (Season, Race, Driver, Stint, PitStop, TyreCompound, ...) grouped into 12 categories, their typed attributes, and 29 relationships with cardinalities.

    Why: a shared, machine-readable vocabulary makes the domain inspectable before any model is trained, and gives every later artefact (OWL file, graphs, tables, validation report) one definition to agree with. The design rule in schema.py is that nothing hard-codes an entity or relationship twice — the ontology, both graphs and all five reports are generated from the same tuples.

    Run it

    python scripts/build_knowledge_base.py

    How it works, step by step

    1. Declare the domain as data

      schema.py defines Entity, Attribute and Relationship as frozen dataclasses and lists the whole domain in two tuples, ENTITIES and RELATIONSHIPS. Each attribute carries a DataType (mapped to XSD later) and each relationship a Cardinality.

    2. Build the OWL ontology

      build_ontology creates one root class per category (suffixed Category so the Weather category cannot collide with the Weather entity), then entity classes — roots first, so a child's parent class always exists. Attributes become DataPropertys named Entity_attribute with an XSD range; relationships become ObjectPropertys. Cardinality is encoded as OWL characteristics: many-to-one and one-to-one are FunctionalProperty, one-to-one is also InverseFunctionalProperty. The result is saved as RDF/XML.

    3. Build two graphs

      build_schema_graph turns the schema into a NetworkX MultiDiGraph (a multigraph, because two entities can be linked by more than one named relationship). build_instance_graph populates a small sample race (the ABox), and instance_graph_to_rdf serialises it as RDF triples with rdf:type and rdfs:label for Turtle export.

    4. Validate the model

      run_all_checks runs the suite in validation.py: unique entity and relationship names, every relationship endpoint exists, every declared parent exists, no orphan entities, and the instance graph conforms to the schema. The driver script exits non-zero on any failure, so it doubles as a CI gate.

    5. Render and report

      visualize.py draws the schema and instance graphs as PNGs and emits a Mermaid source file; reports.py writes the entity, attribute, relationship, ontology and validation tables as Markdown.

    Technologies

    TechnologyWhy and how it is used
    owlready2Creates OWL classes and properties as Python objects and writes RDF/XML that Protégé or any OWL reasoner can open. Chosen because the ontology is generated from code, not drawn by hand.
    rdflibBuilds the instance graph as RDF triples and serialises Turtle (.ttl), the format SPARQL tools expect.
    NetworkXGraph structure, summary statistics and GraphML export of both graphs.
    matplotlibStatic PNG renders of the graphs, coloured by category.
    dataclasses + EnumFrozen, typed domain declarations — the single source of truth.

    Key functions

    build_ontologyapp/intelligence/knowledge_representation/ontology.py:62Generates and saves the OWL ontology from the schema.

    Applications

    • Open formula1.owl in Protégé to browse the class hierarchy or run a reasoner.

    • Use the entity/attribute tables as the data dictionary for Practicals 4 and 5.

    Key points & viva

    Why generate every deliverable from one schema?

    Single source of truth: the tables, the ontology and both graphs all derive from schema.py, so adding an entity or relationship in one place updates every deliverable on the next run.

    How is cardinality represented in OWL?

    Many-to-one and one-to-one relationships become FunctionalProperty; one-to-one is also InverseFunctionalProperty, so an OWL reasoner can enforce the intended multiplicity.

    Why is the instance validation subclass-aware?

    _subclass_closure resolves each entity's descendants, so an edge whose declared range is TrackStatus legitimately accepts a SafetyCar individual.

    What does an entity's source field record?

    Whether it comes from the Kaggle historical schema, FastF1, or both — provenance carried into the data-engineering practical.

    Practical 2 of 10 · app/intelligence/expert_system/

    Rule-Based Expert System

    32 production rules with forward and backward chaining, and an explanation for every firing.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplicationsKey points & viva

    What and why

    Practical 2 encodes race-strategy expertise as 32 IF–THEN rules in 10 categories (weather, safety car, tyre, pit, strategy, ...), and an inference engine that derives decisions such as pit_decision, recommended_tyre and risk_level from a race state.

    Why: some strategy knowledge is categorical and well understood — a safety car makes a stop cheap, standing water needs full wets — and a statistical model trained on one dry race could never learn it. Rules also explain themselves: every derived fact records which rule produced it and which conditions held. In Practical 9 the rule verdict takes precedence over the ML models for exactly this reason.

    Run it

    python scripts/run_expert_system.py

    How it works, step by step

    1. Rules are data, not if-statements

      rules_schema.py defines Condition (fact <operator> value), Action (set key = value, with an optional confidence) and Rule (conditions, connective ALL/ANY, actions, salience). rule_base.py lists the rules with the rule(), cond() and act() shorthands.

    2. Closed-world condition evaluation

      Condition.evaluate returns False for a missing or None fact and for incomparable types, so a rule never fires on data it does not have.

    3. Working memory with provenance

      WorkingMemory stores each fact with its provenance (input or derived) and the rule that asserted it. assert_fact returns whether memory actually changed — the signal the engine uses to detect a fixed point.

    4. Forward chaining (data-driven)

      Each iteration, forward_chain collects every satisfied rule (the conflict set), orders it by the chosen strategy — by default salience, then specificity (more conditions wins), then rule id — and fires the rules that still change memory. A rule/value signature stops identical re-firings. It stops at a fixed point or after 200 iterations. notes accumulate instead of overwriting.

    5. Backward chaining (goal-driven)

      backward_chain proves a goal such as pit_decision == 'PIT_NOW': it finds rules that assert it, checks each condition against the facts, recurses on equality conditions it cannot yet satisfy, and returns a ProofNode tree. A visited set stops cycles.

    6. Validate and explain

      validate_rule_base checks unique ids, non-empty rules, registered fact keys, operator/value sanity, confidence bounds, and contradictions (identical antecedents and salience asserting different values). Explainer.justify answers how a fact was derived: the rule, the conditions that held and the supporting facts.

    Technologies

    TechnologyWhy and how it is used
    Pure PythonNo rule-engine library: the engine is ~270 lines, so its conflict resolution and fixed-point logic are visible and unit-tested.
    dataclasses (frozen) + EnumImmutable, hashable rules and type-safe operators.
    operator moduleMaps each Operator to a comparison function (_OPS).
    JSON exportrule_base.json makes the rule base readable outside Python.

    Key functions

    Function / classLocationRole

## Inputs (GIVEN facts)

| Fact | Value |
|------|-------|
| `track_status` | 'SC' |
| `tyre_wear` | 52 |
| `in_pit_window` | True |
| `current_position` | 5 |
| `laps_remaining` | 30 |
| `weather_severity` | 'dry' |

## Firing sequence

| # | Iter | Rule | Name | Asserted |
|---|------|------|------|----------|
| 1 | 1 | `R-SC-001` | Safety car deployed + worn tyres -> pit now | pit_decision='PIT_NOW', notes='SC out: cheap pit stop, pit immediately.' |

## Conclusions (derived decisions)

| Decision | Value |
|----------|-------|
| `pit_decision` | 'PIT_NOW' |
| `notes` | 'SC out: cheap pit stop, pit immediately.' |

## WHY — narrative explanation

```
The engine fired 1 rule(s) over 2 iteration(s) and reached a stable conclusion.
  [iter 1] R-SC-001 «Safety car deployed + worn tyres -> pit now» fired, asserting pit_decision='PIT_NOW', notes='SC out: cheap pit stop, pit immediately.' — Under a safety car the pit-loss shrinks dramatically; stopping with worn tyres is near free time.
Final decisions:
  • pit_decision = 'PIT_NOW'
  • notes = 'SC out: cheap pit stop, pit immediately.'
```

## HOW — per-decision justification

…
    Limitation to know

    The live pipeline populates 16 input keys. The evaluation run of 2026-10-01 found 10 of 32 rules condition on keys it never fills, so they are correct in isolation but cannot fire through /api/strategy/predict (artifacts/evaluation/domain_validation.json).

    Applications

    • Encoding pit-wall policy (safety-car stops, weather changeovers) that must hold regardless of what the data says.
    • Auditable decisions: every recommendation carries the rules that produced it.
    • The live strategy pipeline (Practical 9) runs forward_chain on every request.

    Key points & viva

    Why 32 curated rules rather than hundreds?

    Near-duplicate rules inflate a count without adding knowledge and create order-dependent conflicts. A smaller, non-redundant base can be validated: validate_rule_base checks unique ids, registered fact keys, operator/value sanity, confidence bounds and contradictions.

    Forward or backward chaining — when is each used?

    Forward chaining derives every conclusion from the race state (the live pipeline uses it); backward chaining starts from a goal such as pit_decision == 'PIT_NOW' and returns a proof tree.

    How is a conflict between satisfied rules resolved?

    By default salience first, then specificity (more conditions), then rule id — a deterministic sort key.

    Practical 3 of 10 · app/intelligence/search/

    State-Space Search

    Pit strategy as a shortest-path problem, solved by BFS, DFS, UCS, Greedy and A*.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplications

    What and why

    Practical 3 casts strategy as search over race states: from lap 0 on the start tyre, choose at every lap whether to run on or pit for a compound, so that the full distance takes the least estimated time.

    Why: the cost structure is a genuine trade-off — softer tyres are faster but degrade sooner, each stop costs 22 s — and search finds the provably optimal plan under an explicit model rather than a heuristic guess. Comparing five algorithms on the same problem shows the optimality/efficiency trade-off with real counts.

    Run it

    python scripts/run_search.py

    How it works, step by step

    1. State

      RaceState is a frozen dataclass: lap, compound, tyre age, stops made, fuel, and the set of compounds used. key() buckets fuel to one decimal so floating-point noise does not split identical states in the explored set.

    2. Actions and transitions

      actions returns RUN, or PIT(compound) for each different allowed compound while stops remain and it is not the last lap. result applies one: a pit stop resets tyre age, adds the compound to the used set and counts the out-lap as a lap.

    3. Cost model

      step_cost is the time the action adds: lap_time = compound base pace + linear degradation (plus an extra 2.5× the degradation rate for every lap past the compound's cliff), scaled up on a track hotter than 30 °C, + a fuel-weight penalty; a pit adds the pit loss to an out-lap on fresh tyres.

    4. Goal

      is_goal requires the full distance and, in a dry race, at least two distinct dry compounds — the real F1 regulation.

    5. Algorithms

      BFS (FIFO) and DFS (LIFO with a depth bound) are uninformed. UCS, Greedy and A* share one _best_first core that differs only in the priority: g(n), h(n) or g(n)+h(n). It uses a heap with a counter tie-breaker for determinism and skips stale entries when a cheaper route to a state was found.

    6. Admissible heuristic

      heuristic = laps remaining × fastest fresh-tyre base pace. No lap can be faster than that, and it ignores degradation, fuel and any mandatory stop, so it never overestimates — which is what makes A* optimal.

    7. Measure

      _instrument wraps each run with time.perf_counter and tracemalloc for wall time and peak memory; comparison.compare tabulates cost gap, nodes expanded and frontier size.

    Technologies

    TechnologyWhy and how it is used
    heapq / collections.dequePriority queue for UCS/Greedy/A*, FIFO queue for BFS.
    dataclasses (frozen)Hashable states for the explored set.
    tracemalloc + perf_counterMeasured, not estimated, time and memory per algorithm.
    NetworkX + matplotlibSearch-tree slice, stint bar and metric charts.

    Data Engineering & EDA

    Load, clean, audit and analyse eight tables, then publish one clean lap table.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplications

    What and why

    Practical 4 turns raw CSVs into an audited, analysed dataset. The lap table fastf1_laps.csv is real: 1,055 laps from 20 drivers at the 2023 Bahrain GP, fetched with FastF1 by scripts/fetch_real_session.py. The seven Kaggle-style tables (results, drivers, pit stops, ...) are synthetic, generated by synthetic.py with deliberately injected problems so the cleaning has something to fix.

    Why: every later practical trains on this output, so cleaning has to be reproducible and every change visible. Each step appends a StepReport to a CleaningReport — an audit trail of rows before/after and what was changed.

    Run it

    python scripts/run_eda.py

    How it works, step by step

    1. Load against a schema

      schemas.py declares every table's columns and their kind (ID, numeric, time, date, categorical, ...). load_csv validates required columns and turns Ergast's \N sentinels into NaN.

    2. Clean, in five audited steps

      clean_table: (1) drop exact duplicates; (2) coerce types and parse m:ss.mmm lap times to seconds with parse_laptime_to_seconds; (3) trim and upper-case categoricals so spelling variants merge; (4) impute numerics by median and categoricals by mode, leaving IDs and dates as NaN; (5) detect IQR outliers (1.5 × IQR) and, as run_eda.py calls it, cap them.

    3. Score quality and summarise

      data_quality produces a 0–100 scorecard; statistical_summary adds skew and kurtosis to describe(); correlation_analysis lists the strongest pairs.

    4. Nine domain analyses

      Driver, constructor, circuit, pit stop, tyre (pace and degradation per compound), lap time, weather, season and safety car (track-status distribution).

    5. Encode and scale (demo)

      encode_and_scale one-hot encodes low-cardinality categoricals, label-encodes the rest and standardises numerics — written out as a demonstration only. Practical 5 deliberately does not reuse scaled data (see its leakage rule).

    6. Publish the hand-off

      The cleaned lap table is published to data/processed/fastf1_laps_clean.csv, and the real-vs-synthetic marker is copied to data_source.json so no later stage has to guess the provenance.

    scikit-learn StandardScalerStandardisation in the encoding demo.
    FastF1Downloads real timing data from F1's live-timing archive.
    matplotlib / seabornFigures and a composite dashboard image.

    Practical 5 of 10 · app/intelligence/features/

    Feature Engineering & Selection

    Candidate features in six blocks, a four-stage selection funnel, and a contract every model reads.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplications

    What and why

    Practical 5 builds candidate features from the clean laps, defines the three targets, and selects 45 features for lap time and 8 for the pit decision over 995 modelling rows. The result is written as a contract — f1_features_selected.csv plus feature_metadata.json — that Practicals 6–10 read instead of hard-coding feature lists.

    Why: two rules protect every later result. No leakage: sector times sum to the lap time (measured by leakage_evidence), and speed traps and IsPersonalBest are only known after the lap, so they are excluded before anything is built. No scaling here: scaling on the full dataset would leak its statistics into every later cross-validation fold, so it is left to Practical 6, inside each fold.

    Run it

    python scripts/build_features.py

    How it works, step by step

    1. Targets

      add_targets adds target_laptime, target_pit_next_lap (1 when the stint index rises on the next lap — the lap before the stop, which is the decision point) and a fuel-corrected lap time from a fitted linear fuel coefficient.

    2. Six feature blocks

      engineer_features, with a recorded reason for each feature: A tyre/stint (tyre life, its square, compound × tyre-life interactions); B race progress; C the driver's own recent pace as gap-to-field, strictly causal via shift(1) before rolling; D field pace (previous-lap median and trend); E environment (air temp, track–air delta, humidity, wind, a mean-centred temperature × tyre-life interaction); F one-hot compound, team and driver with one reference level dropped.

    3. Trim the warm-up

      trim_warmup drops opening laps where history features are undefined, keeping the two frames aligned row for row.

    4. Funnel stage 1–3

      Near-zero variance (near_zero_variance), then correlation above 0.95 — mutual information decides which of a pair survives (prune_correlated) — then VIF ≤ 10 on continuous columns only (prune_by_vif; a rare dummy always looks collinear with its group). On this data the funnel dropped: is_rainfall (near zero variance), tyre_life_sq (correlation), air_temp (correlation), track_air_delta (correlation), race_progress (vif).

    5. Funnel stage 4 — rank and choose K

      rank_features averages three notions of importance by rank: mutual information, random-forest importance and the L1 (Lasso / L1-logistic) coefficient. rank_with_stability records how many lap-forward folds put each feature in their top 12. choose_regression_features sweeps K and keeps the smallest K within 2% of the best CV MAE; classification fixes K = 8 because ~5% positives make a sweep noise.

    6. Write the contract

      build_metadata records the selected features per target, each feature's provenance, which features need scaling, the leakage exclusions and the validation strategy; FeatureContract gives later code a typed view over it.

    Technologies

    scikit-learnMutual information, RandomForest, LassoCV / L1 logistic regression, LinearRegression (VIF and fuel coefficient).
    pandas groupby / shift / rollingPer-driver, strictly causal history features.
    Lap-forward expanding splitsThe same time-ordered validation shape Practical 6 uses.

    Practical 6 of 10 · app/intelligence/ml/

    Machine Learning

    10 classical models, time-aware validation, tuned thresholds and a generalisation guard.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplicationsKey points & viva

    What and why

    Practical 6 trains and compares classical models for both targets: linear/logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, SVR/SVM and XGBoost. The selected lap-time model is svr (test MAE 0.781 s, R² 0.302) and the selected pit model is random_forest (test PR-AUC 0.250 at a tuned threshold of 0.4803).

    Why it is built the way it is: the data is a time-ordered panel, so a shuffled K-fold would train on lap 50 and validate on lap 10. Every model is validated on expanding-window, lap-forward folds and tested once on a chronological holdout (the last 20% of laps). Scalers are fitted inside each fold's pipeline. Pit stops are rare, so ROC-AUC alone would flatter the classifiers; PR-AUC, F1 and a tuned threshold are reported alongside it.

    Run it

    python scripts/build_all.py   # or: python -c "from app.intelligence.ml import pipeline; pipeline.train_all()"

    How it works, step by step

    1. Load and police the contract

      data_contract.load_and_validate checks that the selected columns exist, that no leakage column is present, and that there are no missing values; build_task_frame makes one frame per target.

    2. Split by time

      chronological_holdout reserves the last 20% of unique laps, keeping whole laps on one side. expanding_window_folds cuts the remaining laps into 5 blocks: fold i trains on blocks 0..i−1 and validates on block i.

    3. Preprocess inside the pipeline

      build_preprocessor is a ColumnTransformer: continuous features are median-imputed and — only for models that need it (linear, SVM) — standard-scaled; binary indicators pass through unscaled. Because it sits inside the sklearn Pipeline, it is re-fitted on each fold's training rows.

    4. Tune

      run_expanding_window_search is a custom grid search rather than GridSearchCV, so a fold that fails (e.g. a single class in training) is recorded as an error instead of aborting, and a fold where a metric is undefined is excluded from the mean, not counted as zero. The winner is refitted on the whole development set.

    5. Tune the decision threshold

      tune_threshold picks the probability cut-off on pooled out-of-fold predictions (never the test set), maximising F1 by default; an expected-cost objective with a missed pit costing 5× an early stop is also supported. 0.5 is only optimal for balanced classes with equal error costs — neither holds here.

    6. Select, with a guard

      rank_regression_models ranks by CV MAE; _apply_generalisation_guard overrides the CV winner only if its holdout R² is negative while another model's is positive — and says so in the report.

    7. Persist and register

      Pipelines are saved with joblib; write_registry records every model in model_registry.json, which the API reads to know which models exist.

    Technologies

    joblibscikit-learn's recommended persistence format for fitted pipelines.
    matplotlibROC / PR curves, confusion matrix, residuals, importance — each with a JSON sidecar of the numbers that drew it.

    Applications

    • POST /api/ml/predict/laptime and /api/ml/predict/pit serve the registered pipelines.
    • The same holdout is reused by Practicals 7, 8 and 10, so results are directly comparable.

    Key points & viva

    Why expanding-window validation instead of K-fold?

    The data is a time-ordered driver × lap panel. Random K-fold would train on later laps and validate on earlier ones, so every score would be optimistic. Lap-forward folds put the model in the situation a real strategy model is in.

    What does a negative test R² mean here?

    The model does worse on the closing laps than predicting the training mean — a different fuel and tyre regime from training, not a bug. The generalisation guard stops such a model being selected when another one generalises.

    Why tune the threshold instead of using 0.5?

    0.5 is only right for balanced classes with equal error costs. Pit stops are 48 of 995 laps, so the cut-off is chosen on pooled out-of-fold predictions.

    Extension — what do the quantum models show?

    Three PennyLane models on the noiseless default.qubit simulator, on the same split and metrics: features PCA-reduced to 4 qubits (81.8% of variance kept). The only defensible claim is a narrow comparison with classical models given the same inputs — not a quantum speed-up, not better models, and nothing about real (noisy) hardware.

    Practical 7 of 10 · app/intelligence/dl/

    Deep Learning

    Two Keras networks, tuned on the same folds and tested on the same holdout as Practical 6.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplicationsKey points & viva

    What and why

    Practical 7 trains a multilayer perceptron per target and tests — rather than assumes — whether it beats Practical 6. The lap-time network (16,257 parameters) reaches test MAE 0.565 s, R² 0.456; the pit network (289 parameters) has test ROC-AUC 0.777 at a tuned threshold of 0.1524.

    Why small networks: there are only ~800 development rows and 48 pit events in the whole dataset. Dropout on every hidden layer, L2 weight decay and early stopping are used together, and the overfitting verdict is computed from the training curves, not asserted.

    Run it

    python -c "from app.intelligence.dl import pipeline; pipeline.train_all()"

    How it works, step by step

    1. Runtime

      prepare_dl_runtime selects Keras 3's PyTorch backend before keras is imported — TensorFlow publishes no wheel for the Python version this project targets.

    2. Build

      _hidden_stack stacks Dense(ReLU) + Dropout layers with an L2 regulariser. build_regression_mlp adds a linear head (MSE or Huber loss); build_classification_mlp adds a sigmoid head (binary cross-entropy).

    3. Class weights inside the loss

      On this Keras/PyTorch install, fit(class_weight=...) was measured not to weight the loss. weighted_binary_crossentropy applies the weights inside the loss instead, and a test asserts it moves the predictions.

    4. Fit one fold

      fit_fold fits the feature scaler on the training rows only, optionally standardises the lap-time target, and trains with EarlyStopping(patience=20, restore_best_weights=True) on validation loss.

    5. One-factor-at-a-time search

      tuning.search starts from a base network and, stage by stage, varies one hyperparameter (architecture, learning rate, batch size, dropout, optimizer, L2, loss — and, for the pit model, whether to class-weight at all) across the CV folds, keeping each stage's winner. Every configuration is logged to the hyperparameter report.

    6. Diagnose the fit

      _diagnose applies stated rules to the saved model's curves: overfit if training MAE is below 60% of validation MAE (regression) or training PR-AUC exceeds validation by 0.25 (classification); underfit if it has not learned the training data. Verdicts: lap time OVERFITTING, pit decision REASONABLE FIT.

    7. Save and verify

      persistence.save recompiles with a standard loss (the custom loss would break the reload), writes the .h5, reloads it and refuses to finish unless the reloaded model reproduces the predictions.

    Key points & viva

    Why is the lap-time target standardised but the binary features are not?

    The target sits around 99.10 s with a standard deviation of 2.01 s; a linear head initialised near zero, under L2 decay, struggles to reach that offset. The target is standardised on training rows and inverted before every metric. Scaling a 0/1 dummy would only cost interpretability.

    How do you know the saved .h5 is the model you trained?

    persistence.save recompiles with a standard loss (the custom class-weighted loss would break the reload), saves, reloads with compile=False, and refuses to continue unless the reloaded model reproduces the predictions within 1e-6. The result is recorded as reload_verified.

    What would you change with more data?

    Hold out whole races rather than the tail of one; try sequence models over stint history; and drop the driver/team identity features to test whether the model generalises to new drivers.

    Practical 8 of 10 · app/intelligence/xai/

    Explainable AI

    SHAP, LIME, counterfactuals, a trust score and per-group performance — for both model families.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplicationsKey points & viva

    What and why

    Practical 8 explains why the Practical 7 networks and Practical 6's selected models predict what they do, globally (which features matter overall) and locally (why this lap). It adds a trust score per prediction and a performance breakdown by driver, team and compound.

    Why several methods: each has a blind spot. SHAP's exact tree explainer is available only for tree models, so the network uses sampled KernelSHAP; LIME is a local linear surrogate that can disagree with SHAP; counterfactuals answer the engineer's actual question ("how many more laps until it says pit?"). Agreement between them becomes one component of the trust score.

    Run it

    python -c "from app.intelligence.xai import pipeline; pipeline.run_all()"

    How it works, step by step

    1. Load what to explain

      loading.load_target loads the network, the classical model and the same holdout. If a model is missing it raises ExplainerUnavailableError — it never substitutes a stand-in. pick_representative_rows chooses laps worth explaining (fastest, slowest, the actual pit lap, the one closest to the decision boundary, ...).

    2. SHAP

      tree_shap gives exact Shapley values for tree ensembles; kernel_shap samples them for the network over a k-means background of 25 points with nsamples=200. global_ranking is mean |SHAP|.

    3. LIME and permutation importance

      lime_analysis.explain_row fits a local surrogate; top_features maps LIME's discretised conditions (tyre_life > 12.00) back to feature names so its top-3 can be compared with SHAP's. permutation_importance measures the score lost when a column is shuffled.

    4. Physically consistent counterfactuals

      tyre_age_scan sweeps tyre age across the training range in 0.5-lap steps. consistent_tyre_age_rows recomputes every feature derived from tyre age (the compound interactions and the temperature interaction) so each probe is a lap that could exist — moving tyre_life alone would not be. DiCE runs as a time-bounded supplementary check.

    5. Trust score

      trust.compute combines confidence (distance from the tuned threshold), agreement between the network and the classical model, SHAP–LIME top-3 Jaccard overlap, and the share of inputs inside the training 1st–99th percentile. Weights are confidence 0.35, model agreement 0.25, explanation stability 0.20, input validity 0.20; a missing component is dropped and the rest renormalised, never scored as zero.

    6. Stratify and narrate

      stratification.stratify and fairness.assess report error or recall per driver, team and compound, flagging small groups; narrative.py writes the plain-English sentence an engineer would read.

    Technologies

    TechnologyWhy and how it is used
    SHAPTreeExplainer (exact) and KernelExplainer (model-agnostic, sampled).
    LIMELocal linear surrogates, used as an independent second opinion.
    DiCE (dice-ml)Diverse counterfactuals, under a wall-clock budget.
    NumPy / pandas / matplotlibScans, tables, waterfalls and stratification plots.

The explainability validation of 2026-10-01 found the per-row top feature track_status moved the prediction by 0.197 s on ablation versus 0.177 s for a random feature.

    Applications

    • POST /api/strategy/predict?explain=true attaches SHAP factors and a trust score to a live recommendation.
    • The Explainability page of the dashboard reads only artifacts/xai/.

    Key points & viva

    How do you know a SHAP explanation is not misleading?

    The tree model uses exact TreeExplainer; the network's sampled KernelExplainer values are labelled approximate (compare rank and sign, not magnitude); LIME runs on the same rows as a second opinion and its local_r2 is reported. SHAP explains what the model does, not what is true — which is why the fairness assessment exists.

    Why SHAP and LIME, and why two SHAP explainers?

    Exact when possible, model-agnostic when necessary. SHAP–LIME disagreement is a signal, and the trust score uses it.

    Is the trust score principled or arbitrary?

    Its components are real failure modes — distance from the tuned threshold, model agreement, explanation agreement, familiar inputs. Its weights (confidence 0.35, model agreement 0.25, explanation stability 0.20, input validity 0.20) are a documented judgement, not a fit, and are exposed in trust.WEIGHTS so they can be challenged.

    Why does DiCE have a time budget?

    Its random search can sample for a long time without finding an opposite-class row when pit laps are rare. It is capped at 60 s, starts from the row closest to the boundary, and stays inside each feature's training range; running out of budget is reported, not hidden.

    A counterfactual says "not reachable" — is that a failure?

    It is a result: sweeping tyre age across its whole training range never crosses the threshold, so the decision depends on combinations of features, not tyre age alone.

    Practical 9 of 10 · app/services/ · app/api/ · frontend/

    System Integration & Deployment

    One strategy pipeline that chains every practical, behind an API, a dashboard and Docker.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplications

    What and why

    Practical 9 turns eight separate capabilities into one product. A race state goes in to POST /api/strategy/predict; a single recommendation (STAY OUT / PIT NOW / PIT IN N LAPS) comes out, with the evidence from every stage attached.

    Why an API and a separate frontend (instead of the lab's suggested Streamlit): the same endpoints back the dashboard, the tests and scripts/demo_predict.py, and a page that invents a number instead of fetching one is obvious.

    Run it

    ./run.sh        # or: docker compose build && docker compose up

    How it works, step by step

    1. Validate

      RaceStateRequest (Pydantic) rejects inconsistent states — current_lap ≤ total_laps, tyre_age ≤ current_lap — and the router checks driver, team, compound and model choices against the live dataset and registry. Failure is a 422.

    2. Construct features

      build_feature_row maps the race state onto the exact selected features: tyre life, race progress, compound one-hots and interactions, driver/team one-hots; anything it cannot derive is median-filled and listed as approximated. _flag_out_of_range warns when a derived value is outside the training range.

    3. ML, rules, DL

      _run_ml predicts with the registered Practical 6 pipelines; _run_expert_system runs Practical 2's forward chaining on a 16-key input dict; _run_dl runs the Practical 7 networks at their tuned threshold (never 0.5).

    4. Search

      _run_search runs A* (Practical 3) over the remaining laps from the current compound.

    5. Recommend

      _combine_recommendation: a fired expert-system pit_decision wins outright; otherwise ML and DL are compared — agreement is used, disagreement is reported (disagreement: true) and falls back to ML. A pit verdict is refined into PIT NOW / PIT IN N LAPS from the A* plan's first pit action.

    6. Explain (opt-in) and report

      With explain=true, Practical 8's explain_feature_row attaches SHAP factors and a trust score. POST /api/strategy/report renders the same analysis as a Markdown or HTML briefing.

    7. Serve and deploy

      app/api/main.py registers the routers, restricts CORS to an allow-list, and mounts only the artifact folders the frontend reads (model files are never served). The Next.js dashboard has a page per area; Dockerfile, frontend/Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml build code-only images with artifacts/ and data/ bind-mounted.

    Practical 10 of 10 · scripts/evaluate_system.py · app/services/rai_service.py · docs/

    Evaluation, Responsible AI & Documentation

    Seven generated evaluation sections, a responsible-AI view, and the project documents.

    What and whyHow it works, step by stepTechnologiesKey functionsCode walkthroughOutputs and examplesApplications

    What and why

    Practical 10 evaluates the integrated system and writes every result to artifacts/evaluation/*.json, so the final report reads numbers from files, never from text typed by hand. The latest run (2026-10-01) passed 301 of 301 tests at 64.5% line coverage; the strategy endpoint answered in 101 ms median, 125 ms at p95.

    Why a script instead of a write-up: a script can be re-run after every change and can fail loudly. Each section is independent; one that cannot run reports "available": false with a reason instead of an invented number.

    Run it

    python scripts/evaluate_system.py   # --skip-pytest for a quick run

    How it works, step by step

    1. Functional testing

      functional_testing runs the real pytest suite with coverage and counts results from its --junitxml output — the plain summary line disappears when coverage reports are requested, so stdout is not scraped.

    2. Performance

      performance_evaluation confirms empirically that Practicals 6 and 7 use the same holdout (_verify_shared_holdout), consolidates every model's metrics, and times 200 strategy requests with and without explanations.

    3. Domain validation

      domain_validation replays the real race lap by lap through the API and compares pit calls with the stops drivers actually made: 934 laps replayed, pit-call precision 0.125, recall 0.872. It also checks which rules can fire through the live pipeline (_rule_base_reachability).

    4. Explainability validation

      explainability_validation checks SHAP top-feature stability, a faithfulness ablation (does removing the top feature move the prediction more than a random one?) and traceability.

    5. Responsible AI

      responsible_ai_assessment measures robustness (how often small perturbations flip the recommendation), per-team/driver/compound performance, transparency and human oversight. rai_service.py serves a live version for the dashboard's Responsible-AI page, with confidence shown only where a model natively produces one (probabilities, tree spread, Monte-Carlo dropout).

    6. Deployment readiness and future work

      deployment_readiness checks Dockerfiles, the health endpoint, the test result and scans for hard-coded metrics; future_enhancements records the plan.

    7. Documentation

      User manual, SRS, SDD, testing report and deployment guide live in docs/ and are consolidated in this study guide's first tab.

    Technologies

    FastAPI TestClientIn-process requests for latency and backtests.
    resource / timePeak memory and request timing.
    matplotlibLatency, robustness and fairness figures.

    Knowledge representation

    Source: artifacts/knowledge_representation/reports/ontology_documentation.md · generated 2026-09-27 · Practical 1 code walkthrough

    Ontology Documentation

    Generated 2026-09-27 17:42 UTC.

    Overview

    The Formula 1 ontology is an OWL 2 ontology generated programmatically from the declarative domain schema (f1kr.schema). It formalises the racing domain as classes (entities), object properties (relationships) and data properties (attributes).

    • Base IRI: http://f1kr.org/ontology/formula1#
    • Classes: 73
    • Object properties: 29
    • Data properties: 90

    Class hierarchy by category

    CarState

    • FuelLoad — Estimated fuel mass on board.
    • EngineMode — Power-unit deployment mode.
    • ERS — Energy Recovery System state.
    • DRS — Drag Reduction System state.

    Competition

    • Season — A Formula One championship year.
    • Race — A single championship round / event weekend.
    • GrandPrix — The recurring named event (e.g. 'Monaco Grand Prix') across seasons.
    • Circuit — A racing venue / track.

    Competitor

    • Driver — A racing driver.
    • Constructor — A constructor / entrant team.
    • Team — The operational team entity that fields cars for a constructor.
    • Car — The chassis + power unit fielded by a team.

    Decision

    • Strategy — A recommended race-strategy plan (pit/tyre/fuel decisions).
    • Prediction — A model prediction over race outcomes.
    • Recommendation — An actionable recommendation surfaced to the race engineer.
    • Optimization — An optimisation result over the strategy search space.

    PitStrategy

    • PitStop — A pit-lane stop performed by a driver.
    • PitWindow — The lap range within which a pit stop is strategically optimal.
    • Stint — A continuous run on one set of tyres between pit stops.

    RaceControl

    • TrackStatus — Overall track status flag state.
    • SafetyCar (subclass of TrackStatus) — Full safety-car deployment.
    • VirtualSafetyCar (subclass of TrackStatus) — Virtual safety-car period.
    • YellowFlag (subclass of TrackStatus) — Yellow-flag caution.
    • RedFlag (subclass of TrackStatus) — Session-stopping red flag.
    • BlueFlag (subclass of TrackStatus) — Blue flag (yield to leaders).
    • RaceControlMessage — An official race-control message.
    • Incident — An on-track incident under investigation.
    • Penalty — A sporting penalty applied to a driver.

    Result

    • Result — A driver's classified result in a race.
    • Position — A position/order value.
    • Points — Championship points value.
    • Championship — A championship classification context.
    • DriverStanding (subclass of Championship) — A driver's championship standing snapshot.
    • ConstructorStanding (subclass of Championship) — A constructor's championship standing snapshot.

    Session

    • Session — An on-track session within a race weekend.
    • PracticeSession (subclass of Session) — A free-practice session.
    • Qualifying (subclass of Session) — A qualifying session.
    • Sprint (subclass of Session) — A sprint race session.

    Telemetry

    • Telemetry — A telemetry sample stream for a lap.
    • Speed (subclass of Telemetry) — Instantaneous car speed.
    • Throttle (subclass of Telemetry) — Throttle application.
    • Brake (subclass of Telemetry) — Brake application.
    • RPM (subclass of Telemetry) — Engine revolutions per minute.
    • Gear (subclass of Telemetry) — Selected gear.

    Timing

    • Lap — A single completed lap by a driver in a session.
    • Sector — One of the three timing sectors of a lap.
    • SectorTime — The measured time for a sector.
    • LapTime — A recorded lap-time measurement.
    • FastestLap — The fastest lap of a driver in a race.
    • Gap — Time gap to a reference car.
    • Interval — Interval to the car directly ahead.
    • Overtake — An on-track position change event.

    Tyre

    • TyreConcept — Abstract root for tyre-related concepts.
    • TyreCompound (subclass of TyreConcept) — A tyre compound (Soft/Medium/Hard/Inter/Wet).
    • TyreLife (subclass of TyreConcept) — Accumulated age/wear of a tyre set.

    Weather

    • Weather — Weather conditions during a session.
    • TrackTemperature (subclass of Weather) — Track surface temperature.
    • AirTemperature (subclass of Weather) — Ambient air temperature.
    • Humidity (subclass of Weather) — Relative humidity.
    • WindSpeed (subclass of Weather) — Wind speed.
    • RainProbability (subclass of Weather) — Probability of rain.

    Cardinality encoding

    Relationship cardinalities are encoded as OWL property characteristics:

    Cardinality OWL characteristic
    *..1 (many-to-one) FunctionalProperty
    1..1 (one-to-one) FunctionalProperty + InverseFunctionalProperty
    1..* (one-to-many) (plain object property)
    *..* (many-to-many) (plain object property)

    Inference Report — Wet weather changeover

    Generated 2026-09-27 17:42 UTC.

    Inputs (GIVEN facts)

    Fact Value
    rain_probability 85
    track_wet True
    current_compound 'SOFT'

    track_status 'GREEN'

    Firing sequence

    # Iter Rule Name Asserted
    1 1 R-WX-002 Track already wet -> intermediates minimum recommended_tyre='INTERMEDIATE', push_advice='conserve'
    2 1 R-WX-001 Heavy rain forecast -> wet tyres risk_level='high', notes='High rain probability: switch to intermediates.'

    Conclusions (derived decisions)

    Decision Value
    recommended_tyre 'INTERMEDIATE'
    push_advice 'conserve'
    risk_level 'high'
    notes 'High rain probability: switch to intermediates.'

    WHY — narrative explanation

    The engine fired 2 rule(s) over 2 iteration(s) and reached a stable conclusion.
  [iter 1] R-WX-002 «Track already wet -> intermediates minimum» fired, asserting recommended_tyre='INTERMEDIATE', push_advice='conserve' — A wet track with moderate rain calls for intermediates and reduced pace until conditions clarify.
  [iter 1] R-WX-001 «Heavy rain forecast -> wet tyres» fired, asserting risk_level='high', notes='High rain probability: switch to intermediates.' — If rain probability exceeds 70%, intermediates are the safe baseline; grip on slicks collapses once the track wets.
Final decisions:
  • recommended_tyre = 'INTERMEDIATE'
  • push_advice = 'conserve'
  • risk_level = 'high'
  • notes = 'High rain probability: switch to intermediates.'

    HOW — per-decision justification

    recommended_tyre = 'INTERMEDIATE' — via R-WX-002 «Track already wet -> intermediates minimum» - because track_wet is_true - because rain_probability <= 90

    push_advice = 'conserve' — via R-WX-002 «Track already wet -> intermediates minimum» - because track_wet is_true - because rain_probability <= 90

    risk_level = 'high' — via R-WX-001 «Heavy rain forecast -> wet tyres» - because rain_probability > 70

    notes = 'High rain probability: switch to intermediates.' — via R-WX-001 «Heavy rain forecast -> wet tyres» - because rain_probability > 70

    Expert system

    Source: artifacts/expert_system/reports/rule_catalogue.md · generated 2026-09-27 · Practical 2 code walkthrough

    Rule Catalogue

    Generated 2026-09-27 17:42 UTC — 32 rules across 10 categories.

    Salience convention: 100 weather-critical · 80 safety-car · 60 pit/deg · 40 tyre · 20-30 tactical · 0 advisory.

    Category: degradation (3 rules)

    R-DEG-001 — High track temp -> increased degradation

    • Salience: 60 · Specificity: 1 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF track_temperature > 40 THEN set tyre_deg_adjustment = 'increase'; set notes = 'Hot track: expect elevated thermal degradation.'
    • Rationale: Track temperatures above ~40°C accelerate thermal degradation, shortening viable stint length.

    R-DEG-002 — Cool track -> reduced degradation, extend stint

    • Salience: 60 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF track_temperature < 25 AND tyre_wear < 60 THEN set tyre_deg_adjustment = 'decrease'; set pit_decision = 'STAY_OUT'; set notes = 'Cool track favours longer stints.'
    • Rationale: Lower surface temperatures reduce degradation, so a longer stint (fewer stops) becomes viable.

    R-DEG-003 — High graining risk + high wear -> pit soon

    • Salience: 60 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF graining_risk == 'high' AND tyre_wear >= 50 THEN set pit_decision = 'PIT_SOON'; set push_advice = 'conserve'; set notes = 'Manage graining: reduce sliding, plan an earlier stop.'
    • Rationale: Graining scrubs grip nonlinearly; conserving and stopping earlier avoids a lap-time collapse.

    Category: energy (1 rules)

    R-ERS-001 — Defending with DRS train -> deploy ERS on straights

    • Salience: 30 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF gap_behind < 1.0 AND drs_enabled is_true THEN set engine_mode_advice = 'deploy_on_straights'; set defend_advice = 'cover_inside_line'; set notes = 'Under DRS threat: deploy ERS to defend the straights.'
    • Rationale: When a rival is within DRS range, biasing ERS deployment to the straights protects against a slipstream pass.

    Category: fuel (2 rules)

    R-FUEL-001 — Fuel short -> lift and coast

    • Salience: 30 · Specificity: 1 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF fuel_margin < 0 THEN set fuel_advice = 'lift_and_coast'; set push_advice = 'conserve'; set risk_level = 'medium'; set notes = 'Under fuel target: save via lift-and-coast zones.'
    • Rationale: A negative fuel margin means the car will not reach the flag at full pace; lift-and-coast recovers margin.

    R-FUEL-002 — Comfortable fuel + soft tyres -> push

    • Salience: 30 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF fuel_margin > 1.5 AND current_compound == 'SOFT' THEN set fuel_advice = 'normal'; set push_advice = 'push'
    • Rationale: With fuel in hand and grippy tyres, converting the surplus into pace is worthwhile.

    Category: pit (4 rules)

    R-PIT-001 — Critical tyre wear -> pit now

    • Salience: 60 · Specificity: 1 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF tyre_wear >= 80 THEN set pit_decision = 'PIT_NOW'; set risk_level = 'high'
    • Rationale: Beyond ~80% wear, lap-time loss and failure risk rise sharply; stop regardless of window.

    R-PIT-002 — In window + undercut threat -> pit now

    • Salience: 60 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF in_pit_window is_true AND undercut_threat is_true THEN set pit_decision = 'PIT_NOW'; set notes = 'Cover the undercut before the rival gains free air.'
    • Rationale: Reacting to an undercut requires pitting on the same lap or the fresh-tyre advantage flips positions.

    R-PIT-003 — Overcut opportunity + clear air -> extend stint

    • Salience: 60 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF overcut_opportunity is_true AND gap_ahead > 2.0 AND tyre_wear < 65 THEN set pit_decision = 'STAY_OUT'; set push_advice = 'push'; set notes = 'Overcut: push in clear air, pit later than rival.'
    • Rationale: With serviceable tyres and clear air, staying out and pushing can leapfrog a rival who stops early.

    R-PIT-004 — Approaching window edge -> prime pit crew

    • Salience: 60 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF in_pit_window is_true AND tyre_wear >= 55 AND tyre_wear < 80 THEN set pit_decision = 'PIT_SOON'; set notes = 'Within window and wearing: prepare to stop.'
    • Rationale: Signals the crew to be ready without committing, keeping flexibility for a safety car.

    Category: risk (2 rules)

    R-RISK-001 — Multiple high-risk factors -> flag high risk

    • Salience: 0 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF tyre_wear >= 75 AND rain_probability > 50 THEN set risk_level = 'high'; set notes = 'Worn tyres and rain risk compound: high uncertainty.'
    • Rationale: Concurrent worn tyres and rain risk multiply strategic uncertainty and warrant a conservative posture.

    R-RISK-002 — Stable dry conditions mid-race -> low risk baseline

    • Salience: 0 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF weather_severity == 'dry' AND track_status == 'GREEN' AND tyre_wear < 50 THEN set risk_level = 'low'
    • Rationale: Green-flag dry running on healthy tyres is the low-risk baseline against which deviations are judged.

    Category: safety_car (4 rules)

    R-SC-001 — Safety car deployed + worn tyres -> pit now

    • Salience: 80 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF track_status == 'SC' AND tyre_wear >= 40 THEN set pit_decision = 'PIT_NOW'; set notes = 'SC out: cheap pit stop, pit immediately.'
    • Rationale: Under a safety car the pit-loss shrinks dramatically; stopping with worn tyres is near free time.

    R-SC-002 — VSC + in pit window -> pit now

    • Salience: 80 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF track_status == 'VSC' AND in_pit_window is_true THEN set pit_decision = 'PIT_NOW'; set notes = 'VSC reduces pit loss: take the stop within the window.'
    • Rationale: A virtual safety car slows the whole field, cutting the relative time lost in the pit lane.

    R-SC-003 — High SC probability + marginal tyres -> delay pit

    • Salience: 80 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF safety_car_probability >= 60 AND tyre_wear < 55 AND track_status == 'GREEN' THEN set pit_decision = 'DELAY_PIT'; set notes = 'Bank on an imminent SC for a cheaper stop.'
    • Rationale: When a safety car looks likely and tyres are not yet critical, delaying can convert a full-price stop into a discounted one.

    R-SC-004 — SC in final laps + leading -> stay out to keep track position

    • Salience: 80 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF track_status == 'SC' AND laps_remaining <= 8 AND current_position <= 3 THEN set pit_decision = 'STAY_OUT'; set defend_advice = 'control_restart'; set notes = 'Track position outweighs tyre delta this late.'
    • Rationale: Late in a race, losing track position to a pit stop is rarely recoverable; hold position and manage the restart.

    Category: strategy (4 rules)

    R-STRAT-001 — Monaco + front row -> one stop

    • Salience: 60 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF circuit == 'Monaco' AND grid_position <= 3 THEN set strategy_stops = 1; set notes = 'Monaco: track position is king, minimise stops.'
    • Rationale: Overtaking at Monaco is exceptionally hard, so protecting track position with a single stop is standard.

    R-STRAT-002 — High overtaking difficulty -> minimise stops

    • Salience: 40 · Specificity: 1 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF overtaking_difficulty == 'high' THEN set strategy_stops = 1; set defend_advice = 'protect_position'
    • Rationale: Where passing is hard, every pit stop risks a position that cannot be won back on track.

    R-STRAT-003 — High deg circuit + low pit loss -> two stops

    • Salience: 40 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF track_temperature > 40 AND pit_loss < 20 AND overtaking_difficulty != 'high' THEN set strategy_stops = 2; set push_advice = 'push'; set notes = 'Cheap stops + high deg reward an aggressive 2-stop.'
    • Rationale: When pit loss is small and degradation high, a two-stop on fresher tyres beats nursing one set.

    R-STRAT-004 — Low SC likelihood + long stint -> plan fixed strategy

    • Salience: 30 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF safety_car_likelihood == 'low' AND total_laps > 50 THEN set notes = 'Low SC prior: commit to a planned strategy, fewer reactive stops.'
    • Rationale: With little chance of a race-altering SC, a pre-planned strategy usually outperforms reactive gambling.

    Category: tactics (3 rules)

    R-TAC-001 — Close behind + faster tyres -> attack

    • Salience: 20 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF gap_ahead < 1.0 AND tyre_age_laps < 10 AND drs_enabled is_true THEN set push_advice = 'push'; set notes = 'Fresh tyres + DRS: attack the car ahead.'
    • Rationale: A fresher-tyred car within DRS range should press the advantage before the tyre delta erodes.

    R-TAC-002 — Big gap both ways -> manage tyres in clear air

    • Salience: 20 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF gap_ahead > 3.0 AND gap_behind > 3.0 THEN set push_advice = 'conserve'; set notes = 'Clear air: manage tyres, no need to push.'
    • Rationale: With no immediate threat or target, conserving tyres extends strategic options later.

    R-TAC-003 — Under pressure + worn tyres -> defensive lines

    • Salience: 20 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF gap_behind < 1.5 AND tyre_wear >= 60 THEN set defend_advice = 'defensive_lines'; set push_advice = 'conserve'; set notes = 'Worn tyres under pressure: defend, protect braking zones.'
    • Rationale: Worn tyres cannot match a fresher pursuer's pace, so positioning and braking-zone control matter most.

    Category: tyre (5 rules)

    R-TYRE-001 — Soft worn -> step to medium

    • Salience: 40 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF current_compound == 'SOFT' AND tyre_wear >= 60 THEN set recommended_tyre = 'MEDIUM'
    • Rationale: When softs degrade, mediums trade a little peak grip for durability over the next stint.

    R-TYRE-002 — Long final stint -> hard compound

    • Salience: 40 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF laps_remaining > 30 AND track_wet is_false THEN set recommended_tyre = 'HARD'
    • Rationale: A long run to the flag favours the hard compound's durability, avoiding a further stop.

    R-TYRE-003 — Short final stint + dry -> soft for pace

    • Salience: 40 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF laps_remaining <= 15 AND track_wet is_false AND tyre_wear >= 40 THEN set recommended_tyre = 'SOFT'; set push_advice = 'push'
    • Rationale: For a short sprint to the flag, the soft's peak grip outweighs its lower durability.

    R-TYRE-004 — Damp but not wet -> intermediates over slicks

    • Salience: 40 · Specificity: 1 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF weather_severity == 'damp' THEN set recommended_tyre = 'INTERMEDIATE'; set push_advice = 'conserve'
    • Rationale: A damp track lacks the grip for slicks but not the water for full wets; intermediates bridge the gap.

    R-TYRE-005 — Medium mid-race baseline in the heat

    • Salience: 40 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF current_compound == 'SOFT' AND track_temperature > 45 AND laps_remaining > 20 THEN set recommended_tyre = 'MEDIUM'; set notes = 'Very hot track: avoid softs for a long middle stint.'
    • Rationale: In extreme heat, softs overheat quickly; mediums give a more stable operating window for a long stint.

    Category: weather (4 rules)

    R-WX-001 — Heavy rain forecast -> wet tyres

    • Salience: 100 · Specificity: 1 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF rain_probability > 70 THEN set recommended_tyre = 'INTERMEDIATE'; set risk_level = 'high'; set notes = 'High rain probability: switch to intermediates.'
    • Rationale: If rain probability exceeds 70%, intermediates are the safe baseline; grip on slicks collapses once the track wets.

    R-WX-002 — Track already wet -> intermediates minimum

    • Salience: 100 · Specificity: 2 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF track_wet is_true AND rain_probability <= 90 THEN set recommended_tyre = 'INTERMEDIATE'; set push_advice = 'conserve'
    • Rationale: A wet track with moderate rain calls for intermediates and reduced pace until conditions clarify.

    R-WX-003 — Standing water / extreme -> full wets

    • Salience: 100 · Specificity: 1 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF weather_severity == 'extreme' THEN set recommended_tyre = 'WET'; set risk_level = 'high'; set push_advice = 'conserve'; set notes = 'Extreme conditions: full wet tyres, expect SC/red flag.'
    • Rationale: Standing water demands full wet tyres for aquaplaning resistance; expect race-control intervention.

    R-WX-004 — Drying track after rain -> prepare slick changeover

    • Salience: 100 · Specificity: 3 · Connective: all
    • Logic: IF current_compound in ('INTERMEDIATE', 'WET') AND track_wet is_false AND rain_probability < 30 THEN set pit_decision = 'PIT_SOON'; set recommended_tyre = 'SOFT'; set notes = 'Track drying: crossover to slicks approaching.'
    • Rationale: On a drying line, the intermediate 'cliff' arrives fast; plan the crossover to slicks before losing seconds/lap.

    Search Algorithm Comparison Report

    Generated 2026-09-27 17:42 UTC.

    Problem instance

    • Race distance: 24 laps
    • Start compound: SOFT
    • Pit loss: 22.0 s
    • Track temperature: 38 °C
    • Conditions: DRY
    • Allowed compounds: SOFT, MEDIUM, HARD
    • Max pit stops: 2

    Metrics

    Algorithm Found Cost (s) Gap Optimal Expanded Generated Max frontier Time (ms) Peak mem (KB) Depth Stops
    BFS yes 2270.66 +0.4% — 1455 1590 135 14.36 927.4 24 1
    DFS yes 2299.93 +1.7% — 24 29 5 0.14 12.4 24 2
    UCS yes 2262.42 0.0% optimal 1589 1723 135 19.18 785.5 24 1
    Greedy yes 2270.66 +0.4% — 26 72 47 0.52 39.8 24 1
    A* yes 2262.42 0.0% optimal 1005 1139 134 13.66 504.5 24 1

    Headline findings

    • Optimal algorithm(s): UCS, A*
    • Fastest wall-clock: DFS
    • Fewest nodes expanded: DFS
    • Leanest frontier (memory): DFS

    Interpretation

    • Uniform-Cost Search (UCS) is provably optimal for non-negative step costs and provides the ground-truth minimum race time.
    • A* matches UCS's optimal cost while expanding fewer nodes, because the admissible heuristic (laps-remaining × fastest-possible lap) focuses the search toward the goal.
    • BFS finds the shallowest goal, which need not be the cheapest when step costs vary (they do here), so it is generally sub-optimal.
    • DFS uses the least memory but returns the first goal it reaches, typically far from optimal.
    • Greedy best-first is fast (few expansions) but ignores accumulated cost, so it is not cost-optimal.

    Optimal strategy

    The optimal strategy found by A* is:

    • Stint 1: laps 0–14 on SOFT (14 laps)
    • Stint 2: laps 14–24 on MEDIUM (10 laps)

    Total estimated race time: 2262.4 s (1 pit stop(s)).

    State-space search

    Source: artifacts/search/reports/heuristic_table.md · generated 2026-09-27 · Practical 3 code walkthrough

    Heuristic Table

    Generated 2026-09-27 17:42 UTC.

    Definition

    h(state) = (total_laps - state.lap) x fastest_possible_lap
    Component Value Where it comes from
    total_laps 24 the problem instance
    fastest_possible_lap 90.0000 s RaceProblem.fastest_possible_lap(): fresh-tyre pace at zero fuel, the fastest lap physically available
    pit_loss (ignored by h) 22.0 s ignoring a non-negative cost keeps h a lower bound
    h(initial state) 2160.00 s 24 laps x 90.00 s

    Why it is admissible

    Two costs are deliberately left out, and both are non-negative:

    1. Tyre degradation. fastest_possible_lap is fresh-tyre pace; a real lap on worn tyres is slower.
    2. Fuel weight and pit loss. Carrying fuel costs time, and a dry race may still require a stop.

    Leaving out non-negative costs can only make h too small, never too large, so h(n) <= true remaining cost everywhere. That is exactly the condition A* needs to return a cost-optimal solution, and it is why A* and uniform-cost search agree below.

    Admissibility checked on the optimal path

    g is the cost paid to reach the state, h the estimate of what remains, and actual remaining the true figure taken from the optimal solution itself. Admissibility requires h <= actual remaining on every row.

    Lap Compound Tyre age g (s) h (s) f = g + h Actual remaining (s) h <= actual
    0 SOFT 0 0.00 2160.00 2160.00 2262.42 yes
    3 SOFT 3 279.72 1890.00 2169.72 1982.70 yes
    6 SOFT 6 559.79 1620.00 2179.79 1702.63 yes
    9 SOFT 9 840.23 1350.00 2190.23 1422.20 yes
    12 SOFT 12 1121.01 1080.00 2201.01 1141.41 yes
    15 MEDIUM 1 1423.60 810.00 2233.60 838.82 yes
    18 MEDIUM 4 1703.19 540.00 2243.19 559.23 yes
    21 MEDIUM 7 1982.80 270.00 2252.80 279.62 yes
    24 MEDIUM 10 2262.42 0.00 2262.42 0.00 yes

    Checked on all 25 states of the optimal path: 0 violations. Admissibility holds, so A*'s solution is cost-optimal.

    Optimal cost: 2262.4206 s. A* expanded 1005 nodes to find it.

    Uniform-cost search, which uses no heuristic, reached 2262.4206 s while expanding 1589 nodes. The two costs agree, which is the empirical check that the heuristic did not cost optimality — it only saved 584 node expansions.

    State-space search

    Source: artifacts/search/reports/state_space_formulation.md · generated 2026-09-27 · Practical 3 code walkthrough

    State-Space Formulation

    Generated 2026-09-27 17:42 UTC.

    Problem as search

    Race-strategy selection is modelled as a shortest-path search whose solution is the sequence of per-lap decisions (run / pit-and-fit-compound) that completes the race distance in minimum estimated total time.

    Formal components

    Component Definition
    State (lap, compound, tyre_age, stops_made, fuel_kg, compounds_used)
    Initial state lap 0, start compound, age 0, 0 stops, full fuel
    Actions RUN (one lap on current tyres); PIT(compound) (fit a new compound, run the out-lap)
    Transition RUN: lap+1, age+1, fuel−burn. PIT: lap+1, new compound at age 1, stops+1, fuel−burn
    Step cost estimated lap time (compound, age, fuel, track-temp) + pit-loss if pitting
    Goal test lap == total_laps and (dry race ⇒ ≥ 2 dry compounds used)

    Cost model

    Lap time is a transparent, deterministic function:

    lap_time = base_pace(compound)
         + deg(compound) · tyre_age · temp_factor      (with a 'cliff' past cliff_age)
         + fuel_kg · fuel_time_penalty

    Softer compounds have lower base_pace (faster) but higher deg (wear faster), creating the pace-versus-durability trade-off that makes pit strategy non-trivial.

    Heuristic (for informed search)

    h(state) = (total_laps − lap) × fastest_possible_lap

    This is admissible: no lap can be completed faster than the fastest fresh-tyre pace at zero fuel, and the heuristic ignores the (non-negative) mandatory pit loss a dry race may still require — so it never overestimates the true remaining cost. Admissibility guarantees A* returns a cost-optimal solution.

    Goals (per the task specification)

    • Maximum points / optimal finish position — approximated here by minimising total race time, the dominant determinant of finishing position in a time-trial sense.
    • Minimum race time — the direct search objective.

    Feature engineering

    Source: artifacts/feature_engineering/feature_engineering_report.md · generated 2026-09-27 · Practical 5 code walkthrough

    Task 5 — Feature Engineering Report

    Generated 2026-09-27 17:43 UTC.

    Input: data/processed/fastf1_laps_clean.csv (Task 4's cleaned laps).
    Output: data/processed/f1_features_selected.csv (995 rows) and data/processed/feature_metadata.json.
    Data source: real_fastf1 — Bahrain 2023 (R).

    1. Engineered features

    50 candidate features were built in six blocks: tyre and stint dynamics, fuel and race progress, the driver's own recent pace in gap-space, field-level pace, environment, and reference-encoded categoricals. Two rules govern all of them: anything derived from history uses shift(1) so no feature can see the lap it predicts, and no feature is an exact linear combination of others.

    The fuel-burn coefficient was estimated from the data at -0.0613 s per lap (negative means the car speeds up as fuel burns off), and used to build the fuel-corrected target.

    2. Leakage exclusions

    Excluded before any feature was built: Sector1Time, Sector2Time, Sector3Time, SpeedFL, SpeedST, IsPersonalBest.

    Reason: Sector times sum exactly to LapTime; speed traps and IsPersonalBest are only knowable during or after the lap being predicted.

    3. The selection funnel

    Stage Removes Dropped here
    1. Near-zero variance constant or near-constant columns 1: is_rainfall
    2. Correlation pruning (|r| > 0.95) one of each redundant pair 3: tyre_life_sq, air_temp, track_air_delta
    3. Variance inflation (VIF > 10) multi-way collinearity 1: race_progress
    4. Importance and stability weak or unstable predictors see the importance report

    Correlated pairs, and which of the two survived (mutual information decided):

    Kept Dropped |r|
    tyre_life tyre_life_sq 0.9561
    race_progress air_temp 0.9803
    race_progress track_air_delta 0.9718

    Removed for multicollinearity, worst first:

    Feature VIF at removal
    race_progress 24.9

    4. What was exported

    • 45 features for target_laptime
    • 8 features for target_pit_next_lap
    • 45 columns exported (the union), plus 5 identifier columns and 3 targets
    • 60 warm-up rows dropped; first usable lap is 4

    5. The contract for later tasks

    • Scaling: NOT applied here. Fit the scaler inside each CV fold to avoid leakage.
    • Validation: Expanding-window lap-forward split; keep whole laps in one fold. Do not use random K-fold - this is a time-ordered panel.
    • Needs scaling: 14 numeric features; 31 binary indicators do not.

    6. Validation scores at selection time

    • Regression CV MAE 0.9891 s, R² 0.4491
    • Classification CV ROC-AUC 0.8969

    48 pit event(s) observed across 21 distinct laps (the busiest lap accounts for 12% of all pits) - a reasonably realistic spread of strategic pit timing. This remains a single session, though, and results should not be generalised beyond it.

    Full step-by-step walkthrough with intermediate tables: docs/notebooks/task5_feature_engineering.ipynb.

    Machine learning & quantum

    Source: artifacts/reports/classical_vs_quantum_report.md · generated 2026-09-27 · Practical 6 code walkthrough

    Classical vs Quantum — Machine Learning on the Same F1 Data

    Generated 2026-09-27 17:57 UTC.

    Simulator: default.qubit (noiseless state-vector simulation; no quantum hardware) · PennyLane 0.45.1 · seed 42 · total run time 27.3 s

    Read this first. These are small variational circuits simulated exactly on a classical computer, trained on one Grand Prix. There is no quantum hardware in this project and nothing here demonstrates a quantum advantage — a noiseless simulation of 4 qubits is something a laptop does easily, which is the whole reason it is possible to run this experiment at all. The comparison is worth making because it is fair: same laps, same splits, same metric code.

    How the comparison was kept fair
    Data the Task 5 feature matrix, loaded through Task 6's own data contract
    Split Task 6's chronological holdout — 815 development laps, 180 test laps
    Cross-validation Task 6's 4 expanding-window lap-forward folds
    Selection hyperparameters chosen on the folds only; the test laps were used once
    Search space layers ∈ [1, 2, 3], learning rate ∈ [0.05, 0.1]
    Metrics app.intelligence.ml.evaluation — the same functions Tasks 6 and 7 call
    Thresholds tuned on pooled out-of-fold predictions, never left at 0.5

    Getting 45 features into 4 qubits

    • Pit decision: PCA to 4 components, retaining 81.8% of the variance.
    • Lap time: PCA to 4 components, retaining 28.7% of the variance.

    Angle encoding needs a bounded range, so features are standardised and mapped to [0, π]. Both the standardiser and the PCA are fitted on training rows only — inside each fold during cross-validation, and on the development laps for the final model.

    This reduction is a real cost, and it is why the table below includes parameter-matched classical models trained on those same reduced inputs. Task 6's model sees every feature; the matched models see exactly what the circuits see.

    Results — same test laps, same metrics

    Pit decision (target_pit_next_lap)

    Test laps contain 1 pit event(s) in 180 laps. Precision, recall and F1 on so few positives are dominated by chance; the cross-validated columns carry far more events and are the better guide.

    Model Family Params Train (s) CV PR-AUC (mean ± sd) CV ROC-AUC Test PR-AUC Test ROC-AUC Test F1 Test precision Test recall Confusion matrix
    vqc quantum 14 0.46 0.3037 ± 0.1912 0.7699 ± 0.1491 0.0080 0.3073 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 [[108, 71], [1, 0]]
    quantum_kernel_svm quantum 413 3.78 0.2127 ± 0.1940 0.6543 ± 0.1889 0.0122 0.5475 0.0000 0.0000 0.0000 [[162, 17], [1, 0]]
    logistic_regression (reduced inputs) classical (parameter-matched) 5 0.00 0.2047 ± 0.1333 0.7162 ± 0.1405 1.0000 1.0000 0.0132 0.0066 1.0000 [[29, 150], [0, 1]]
    tiny_mlp (reduced inputs) classical (parameter-matched) 13 0.02 0.1529 ± 0.0883 0.7066 ± 0.1344 0.0137 0.7989 0.0118 0.0060 1.0000 [[12, 167], [0, 1]]
    random_forest — Task 6, all selected features classical (full) — not measured here 0.3863 ± 0.1249 0.8482 ± 0.0560 0.2500 0.9832 0.0833 0.0435 1.0000 [[157, 22], [0, 1]]

    A test PR-AUC of 1.0 in that table is not a triumph: with a single positive lap, PR-AUC is 1.0 whenever that one lap happens to receive the highest score, and near 0.01 whenever it does not. The same one lap drives every test precision, recall and F1 value here. Use the CV columns.

    quantum_kernel_svm's parameter count is its SVM dual coefficients plus the intercept — the quantum part of that model is the kernel, which has no trained parameters at all. It is not comparable to the variational circuits' angle counts.

    Lap time (target_laptime)

    Model Family Params Train (s) CV MAE (mean ± sd) CV R² Test MAE (s) Test RMSE (s) Test R²
    vqr quantum 14 0.45 1.7459 ± 0.3706 -0.1188 ± 0.2759 1.1044 1.4866 -0.4562
    linear_regression (reduced inputs) classical (parameter-matched) 5 0.00 1.6243 ± 0.3357 -0.1015 ± 0.3086 0.9459 1.3355 -0.1753
    tiny_mlp (reduced inputs) classical (parameter-matched) 13 0.00 1.7697 ± 0.2388 -0.1636 ± 0.2548 1.6813 1.8963 -1.3695
    svr — Task 6, all selected features classical (full) — not measured here 1.3813 ± 0.5584 0.2553 ± 0.3918 0.7815 1.0290 0.3023

    The three quantum models

    vqc — AngleEmbedding + StronglyEntanglingLayers, PauliZ expectation through a sigmoid

    • 4 qubits, 1 entangling layer(s), learning rate 0.1, 80 epochs (Adam)
    • 14 trainable parameters, final fit in 0.46 s
    • decision threshold 0.6519 tuned on 635 out-of-fold predictions (36 pit laps): F1 0.1552 at 0.5 → 0.3146 at the tuned value

    quantum_kernel_svm — fidelity kernel ||^2 (2 feature-map reps) + SVC(kernel='precomputed')

    • 4 qubits, 2 feature-map repetitions, C=1.0
    • 413 trainable parameters, final fit in 3.78 s
    • decision threshold 0.8202 tuned on 635 out-of-fold predictions (36 pit laps): F1 0.1429 at 0.5 → 0.2449 at the tuned value
    • 412 support vectors; kernel matrix 815×815

    vqr — AngleEmbedding + StronglyEntanglingLayers, PauliZ expectation scaled to a standardised lap time

    • 4 qubits, 1 entangling layer(s), learning rate 0.1, 80 epochs (Adam)
    • 14 trainable parameters, final fit in 0.45 s

    Discussion

    Pit decision. The best quantum model on cross-validation is vqc (CV PR-AUC 0.3037), which is ahead of the parameter-matched classical model logistic_regression (reduced inputs) (0.2047) on the identical reduced inputs. Task 6's random_forest, which sees every selected feature, reaches 0.3863 on the same folds.

    On the test laps every classifier is judged on 1 pit event(s), so the test columns should not decide anything. That limitation is the dataset's, not the models'.

    Lap time. vqr reaches CV MAE 1.7459 s against 1.6243 s for linear_regression (reduced inputs) on the same 4 PCA components — worse than the matched classical model by 0.122 s. Test MAE is 1.1044 s for the circuit and 0.7815 s for Task 6's svr on all features.

    A circuit whose output is a single Pauli-Z expectation is bounded in [-1, 1] and has a few dozen parameters, so it is closer in capacity to a linear model than to Task 6's ensembles or Task 7's network. Reading it as "quantum is worse than classical" would be the wrong lesson; reading it as "a 26-parameter model with 4 compressed inputs cannot match a 45-feature ensemble" is the right one.

    What this experiment cannot tell you

    • Nothing about quantum advantage. default.qubit simulates the circuit exactly. Any speed comparison in the table favours whichever model has fewer parameters to fit, not whichever is running on better hardware — there is no quantum hardware here.
    • Nothing about scaling. 4 qubits and a 16-dimensional state space is small enough to simulate in milliseconds. The interesting regime starts where simulation stops being possible, and this dataset never gets there.
    • Nothing generalisable about F1. One race, one circuit, 995 laps, one labelled pit stop in the holdout. Every caveat that applies to Tasks 6-8 applies here too.
    • Noise is absent. Real devices decohere. A model that trains cleanly in simulation may not survive contact with hardware, and this project makes no claim that it would.

    Reproducing this

    python scripts/run_qml.py            # writes every artifact below
python scripts/build_all.py          # includes the quantum stage (skip it with --skip-qml)

    Artifacts: artifacts/models/qml/ (weights and config), artifacts/metrics/qml_metrics.json, artifacts/figures/qml_*.png, and this report.

    Task 6 — Pit-Decision Classification Report

    Generated: 2026-09-27T17:43:32.997622+00:00

    Objective

    Predict target_pit_next_lap (should the driver pit at the end of this lap?) from information available before the lap starts.

    Dataset: Real FastF1 session — Bahrain 2023 (R), 1055 laps, 20 drivers

    48 pit event(s) observed across 21 distinct laps (the busiest lap accounts for 12% of all pits) - a reasonably realistic spread of strategic pit timing. This remains a single session, though, and results should not be generalised beyond it.

    This is a single real Grand Prix session. Results reflect genuine race strategy variation but should not be generalised beyond this one race.

    Pit events are rare in every session. As a direct consequence:

    • Some CV folds can have zero pit events in their training split (a classifier cannot be fit on a single class there) or zero pit events in their validation split (ROC-AUC/PR-AUC are mathematically undefined there) — see the per-fold table below for this run.
    • The final chronological holdout test set contains pit events, so test-set ROC-AUC/PR-AUC are defined for every trained model below.

    Excluded as leakage (Task 5 contract): Sector1Time, Sector2Time, Sector3Time, SpeedFL, SpeedST, IsPersonalBest.

    Reason: Sector times sum exactly to LapTime; speed traps and IsPersonalBest are only knowable during or after the lap being predicted.

    Expanding-window, lap-forward cross-validation with a chronologically later, untouched holdout test set. Random K-fold is never used — see app.intelligence.ml.splits.

    6. Models

    Linear/Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, SVM/SVR, and XGBoost (optional — see section 9).
